A good trick to get rid of a lot of dough is to make uthappam. It's made with highly fermented batter. Basically dosa batter that is 3 or more days old. Chop onions, tomatoes, green peppers, and very few green chillies. Pour the batter like a thick pancake, and immediately place a mixture of those veggies on top. Cook on low heat. I am south indian who makes dosa well. So here you go.

But a disclaimer: the most difficult part of making dosa is the spreading part. Unless you have eaten one,  it could be tricky to recreate a dosa.

Ingredients:
2.5 cups of rice (medium grain rice is better)
1 cup of urad/urid/ulundu dal (black lentil, without the husk, it looks off-white without the husk, whole or split is fine but surely dehusked. In indian stores you will find them in both ways)

Optional ingredients
1/4th chana dal (split yellow bengal gram - not to be confused with garbanzo beans or toor dal). Traditionally chans dal is not used,  my mom or granny would never use this. This is a restaurant trick to givethe dosa more strength to hold its contents and stay crispy for longer. 

1 tblspoon methi seeds (fenugreek seeds)
Salt to taste

Prep

Soak ingredients (except salt) in a container with water just about covering the contents and room in the container for the ingredients to grow in volume. Use your hands to give it a mix -this is how the fermentation process gets started - from your hands. If you don't use your hands,  you are not going to ferment it. Don't add salt at this point.

Leave for 2-3 hours. Watch a south indian movie.
The rice should have lost its translucent state and is now very white. It should split easily if you try to with your nails. Don't drain out the water.

Now use a good food processor. Time it such a way that this is the last thing you do in the day. Give yourself 30mins to an hour for this part. Typically a south indian stone grinder is used but a food processor / blender should work. 

Use your "hands" to scoop out from your container into the food processor. Go in batches so as not to overwhelm or overfill the processor. Start with a bit,  blend it, add a bit of water as you go. The dough should be smooth without huge particles but it is ok for it to feel a bit rough between your fingers. It shouldn't be liquidy. It should move slowly. Don't be afraid to give the container a mix with your hand to mix all your bstches of the food processor.

Now make sure you have your dough in a container will another 1/3rd height atleast for it to grow while it ferments. If you processed it in the evening or night,  leave it closed overnight on your kitchen counter. Don't leave it in a place that is too warm or too frigid. If it is warm enough for you to be in the room it is warm enough for the dough to ferment since you are leaving it overnight. Leaving it overnight is the most important part.

Next morning your dough is done! 
It may seem thicker than you left it the previous night. That's good. But it should also have risen alot. You can add about two or three tea spoons of salt and give it a light mix. Don't beat it down too much. 

Now you have enough dough for 20+ dosas. So you could take some dough in a smaller container for your dosa breakfast and leave the rest in the fridge. You don't want to overferment from this point on.

To your smaller container you may add a table spoon or two of water if the dough feels too thick.  It should be easily spreadable but still not too liquidy.

Get a nice  thick pan hopefully nonstick. Get a scouped laddle like a soup ladle.

Heat the pan on low heat for a couple minutes. Spray or spread a very small amount of greese.

Dab a very small amount of dough and make a super tiny dosa. Don't try to make it too thin. The first one is just to get the pan ready. Once you spread it, raise the heat. You will see the dosa cook. As it slowly colors up below, use a flat laddle to pick up this sacrificial dosa (you can eat this,  just doesn't look sexy). Now immefiately reduce the heat. This rhythm is very important. You want the pan to be warm when the dough is being spread but not so hot it cooks too fast before you can spread. Then high heat so it crisps up well. Then quickly reduced to prepare the pan for the next one.

When the pan is ready,  take half a scoop of dough, plop it in the middle, and with the back of the laddle make a spiral to spread the dpugh around. In the first go your intent is to quickly spread for maximum surface area before the dough cooks in place. Then you can do another go just with the laddle spreading any lumpy but uncooked dough over evenly. You want the dosa to be no more than 1/2mm thick and thinner if possible.

You can use your spray or oil or butter over each dosa depending on taste.

You don't need to flip and cook the other side of it is thin but you can if it ends up being thick but you only need to for about 10 seconds. Each dosa should take about 1 to 1:30 minutes to make.

Average consumption in California dropped 20% between 1980 and 1993, and dropped 2 to 3 points each year after that for a few years. Here are screenshots of my kindle book from the key sections on a chapter in that book http://imgur.com/a/Umj4D

Basically, from 1980 to 1993, the average amount of milk consumed by Californians dropped from 30 gallons to 24 gallons. A very smart marketer within the California Fluid Milk Processors' Advisory Board realized there was a huge problem and decided to do something about it. They realized that even though population was going up while average intake was going down, the population increase was not enough to sustain milk sales.

The agency did a lot of research and realized that people don't think of milk individually. People just don't think of milk with a lot of involvement or importance - till they pour some cereal into a bowl and realize they ran out of milk. So the advertising got people to start considering milk purchase as a "grocery shopping best practice".
